title.narrative: Giving for Change 2021

description.narrative: - International NGOs- Funders (bilateral, public and private)- Research institutes and universities

The aim of Giving for Change is to foster local giving as an expression of voice, civic participation, solidarity and dissent. The programme will build evidence around new thinking, approaches and leadership that support community philanthropy development.

To influence and partner with international development actors to appreciate, support and promote the development of communityphilanthropy as a central pillar of broader efforts to shift power and resources closer to the ground, to strengthen local ownership of development processes and to amplify the ability of citizens and communities to be heard and to claim rights and entitlements.Specific objectives include: - Build on, engage and collaborate with other sector-based initiatives aimed at addressing long-term systemic reform of the international development system.- Grow the visibility, voice and influencing power of southern civil society actors and leaders in the #ShiftThePower movement so that they can participate more fully and have greater voice in conversations and processes aimed at reforming aid.- Promote and foster new ways of working that leverage actors and assets on both emergent (community philanthropy, #ShiftThePower) and mainstream (funders and INGOs) sides of the system.

comment.narrative: At the beginning of the Giving for Change programme, the baseline was 0.

In 2021, the GFCF contributed to 2 high level processes that illustrated funders' increased interest in the community philanthropy field, including:- GFCF staff and partners contributed to thinking/discussions behind BOND report "Catalysing Locally-Led Development in the UK Aid System."- GFCF co-organized two online sessions in advance of the UN General Assembly, hosted by hosted by ODI in partnership with the 17 Rooms initiative, SHOFCO and Sharing Strategies. The sessions looked at "advocating together for localization, locally and community-led development and shifting power."Additionally, over the year we were in regular contact with a range of government officials, individual donors and emerging philanthropic actors with the aim of influencing practice (including, for example, the European Commission).

In 2022, the GFCF engaged with a number of new donors, illustrating funders' increased interest in the community philanthropy field. This included the H&S Davidson Trust, Choose Love, Open Society Foundations, GlobalGiving and Porticus. Most significantly, the GFCF received a grant from Mackenzie Scott. Other examples include the UK Humanitarian Innovation Hub publishing the report "Enabling the Local Response: Emerging Humanitarian Priorities in Ukraine", which referenced #ShiftThePower and community philanthropy in the section on "innovative approaches."

In 2023, the GFCF engaged with a number of new donors, illustrating funders' increased interest in the community philanthropy field. This included the Fund for Shared Insight,Global Greengrants Fund, Hilton Foundation and Robert Bosch Foundation (amongst others).

In 2024, the GFCF engaged with a number of new donors, illustrating funders' increased interest in the community philanthropy field. This included working on "meaningful participation" with Porticus' partners, a new funding relationship with the Hans Wildorf Foundation, etc.
In 2025, the GFCF engaged with a number of new donors, illustrating funders' increased interest in the community philanthropy field.
